overview: Malagasy history brings together varied communities and long-distance connections. Research into ancestry finds both African and Asian contributions, with regional differences. No single family custom, craft or royal dynasty represents everybody on the island.

periods.title: Early communities and Indian Ocean exchange
periods.summary: Early settlements and imported ceramics show connections across the Indian Ocean. Northern communities developed stone-vessel production. The map’s year 800 is not a certain date for the first people arriving, and its endpoint in 1000 does not mark their disappearance.

periods.title: A regional manuscript tradition
periods.summary: Manuscripts from southeastern Madagascar preserve Malagasy written in Arabic characters on locally made paper. The Bibliothèque nationale de France dates several examples to the sixteenth century. This was a particular regional tradition, not evidence that everyone on the island could read.

periods.title: French colonial rule
periods.summary: Madagascar became a French colony in 1896. Colonial government changed political authority; it did not begin or end Malagasy identity.

periods.title: Communities in an independent country
periods.summary: Madagascar gained independence in 1960. The modern state and its diverse communities have related histories, but they are different kinds of identity.

periods.title: Recognition for Zafimaniry woodcraft
periods.summary: Zafimaniry woodcraft entered UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008, following recognition in 2003. The inscription honours an existing tradition of building, carving and transmitting practical knowledge.

periods.title: A living art of speaking together
periods.summary: Malagasy kabary entered UNESCO’s Representative List in 2021. The recognition concerns a continuing art of public speech and family participation, not a newly invented custom.

sections.title: A cooking pot with its own feet

items.text: Northern Madagascar’s stone-vessel industry flourished during the centuries around 800 to 1500. Tripod pots from Vohémar have three feet that could hold the bowl over a fire. Soot and burnt residues show heating, while finds in settlements support everyday use alongside burial uses. The residues have not established exactly what every pot contained.

Broken stone pots were sometimes repaired instead of discarded. At Vohémar, two surviving examples were held together with iron bands and mortar. Other fragments have drilled holes for joining pieces with metal clamps. Repairs show the value placed on keeping a vessel useful. A cracked pot could get another chance, though a repaired pot was not necessarily watertight.

The Bibliothèque nationale de France describes manuscripts from southeastern Madagascar written in Arabic characters to record Malagasy. Several are on locally made Antaimoro paper. Writing systems can travel and be adapted to a different language: using Arabic letters does not mean that the words on every page are Arabic. These manuscripts preserve a regional tradition of keeping knowledge in writing.

One volume, catalogued as Malayo-polynésien 285, combines Antaimoro paper with a binding of zebu hide. The record identifies both the writing surface and the cover. A book is also a made object, requiring materials and practical skills as well as words. This particular binding does not tell us how every Malagasy book was produced.

Zafimaniry builders in Madagascar’s southeastern highlands use wooden joints in which a shaped end fits into a matching opening. UNESCO describes houses and tombs assembled without metal nails or hinges. Different tree species suit different jobs. Good building depends on knowing the material as well as making the pieces fit; this tradition has a great deal of knowledge tucked into its joints.

Carving appears on Zafimaniry walls, window frames, stools, chests and tools. Some patterns have named meanings: UNESCO describes a spider’s-web motif associated with family ties and a honeycomb with community life. The decoration can therefore carry ideas about relationships as well as display skill. These meanings belong to this tradition, rather than being a dictionary for every pattern across Madagascar.

sections.title: A game with room for the pieces

items.text: A fanorona board in Islington’s educational handling collection is made from light wood, with black lines and little side drawers for the playing pieces. Two players move along the board’s lines and try to capture their opponent’s pieces. This collected example uses plastic pieces, so it illustrates a continuing game rather than an ancient excavated set. Even a strategy game benefits from somewhere to put everything away.

The same collection tells a story about Prince Andriantompokoindrindra, who was so absorbed in fanorona that he failed to return to his father and lost the chance to become king. It is presented here as a traditional story, not a verified explanation of a royal succession. It certainly gives the familiar request to stop playing a game unusually high stakes.

sections.title: Family gatherings with words worth practising

items.text: Kabary is an art of public speaking using proverbs, carefully arranged phrases and wordplay. It commonly involves two speakers addressing a gathering, and some performances last hours. Skill lies in choosing and arranging words for the occasion. A speech can be something people come together to enjoy, rather than merely an announcement before the interesting part.

Kabary also belongs at family gatherings where several generations take part. UNESCO describes growing participation by women and younger people in an art formerly associated especially with older elite men. A tradition can continue while the people who perform it change. Listening, joining in and learning how to speak are part of its social life.

sections.title: Many family histories, more than one kind of evidence

items.text: A 2017 genetic study sampled 2,704 people in 257 Malagasy villages. Its results supported ancestry connected with both eastern Africa and Southeast Asia, with differences across the island. Such research can help investigate population history, but it does not identify the family who owned an excavated pot or decide somebody’s cultural identity. Archaeology, languages and community histories ask related questions using different evidence.

ending.text: Malagasy peoples continue today, with local traditions, shared connections and changing ways of life. Living practices such as kabary show participation across generations. The map’s endpoint in 1000 is not an extinction date, nor the end of Malagasy culture.
